extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of sociology and political theory; educated general readers interested in the development of political institutions
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis of the factors that further or hinder political integration (the formation and consolidation of larger social/political aggregates). Surveys environmental, physical, moral, and intellectual conditions with historical and ethnographic examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Climate and soil fertility
rubrics_metrics.description: How political integration is prevented by an inclemency of climate, or an infertility of soil, which keeps down population.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cold, raw, or otherwise harsh climates and infertile soils reduce population density and hinder formation of large social aggregates. Examples: Seminoles "so thinly scattered over a barren desert" and certain Snake Indians whose paucity of game causes an "almost entire absence of social organization."

rubrics_metrics.name: Population massing / density
rubrics_metrics.description: The massing of men together within an occupied area is necessary for the formation of larger political aggregates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regions that permit larger numbers of people to concentrate (because of fertility, climate, or lack of dispersing pressures) enable greater social and political integration. Conversely, low population density impedes integration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniformity of surface, mineral products, flora, and fauna
rubrics_metrics.description: Great uniformity of surface, of mineral products, of flora, of fauna, are impediments to political integration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When environment lacks diversity of resources or features that foster specialization and trade, individual prosperity and the interdependence needed for social growth are reduced. The 'special characters' of flora and fauna influence individual prosperity required for social growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure of habitat and ease of communication
rubrics_metrics.description: The structure of the habitat, as facilitating or impeding communication, affects the size of the social aggregate formed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ease of internal communication (roads, navigable routes) increases political integration; barriers (mountains, deserts, marshes, seas) impede it. Examples: Polynesian islands (restricted by seas but consolidated within islands), ancient Peru (valleys separated by deserts/mountains), Grant's remark on equatorial Africa: no jurisdiction extends beyond districts uncrossable in three or four days. Historical note: formation of roads since Roman times made larger aggregates possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Escape/defensive possibilities (security from coercion)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ability of people to escape governmental coercion influences the ease of consolidating political authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Populations able to retreat to other fertile regions resist consolidation; populations 'penned in by barriers' are more easily consolidated. Example: difference attributed by Cieza between ancient Peruvian peoples and neighboring Indians of Popayan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical constitution and inherited vigor
rubrics_metrics.description: A certain type of physique (constitutional energy) is requisite for continuous labor and hence for civilized life and massing of men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Civilized life demands sustained physical energy which is not quickly acquired but slowly inherited through generations. Evidence: Jesuit Paraguay Indians who adopted industrial habits became infertile—suggesting taxation of physique beyond constitution. Thus inherited physical capacity affects a group's potential for integration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral dispositions toward subordination or independence
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain moral traits favor, and others hinder, the union of men into large groups—particularly dispositions toward subordination or mutual hostility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peoples with dispositions like solitary aggression ('two cannot dwell in one den') resist aggregation, while peoples who admire and yield to coercion facilitate it. Examples: Abors similar to 'tigers' who cannot dwell together; Damaras who 'court slavery' and 'follow a master as spaniels would.' These contrasted dispositions largely determine possibility of political integration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nomadic instinct / wandering habits
rubrics_metrics.description: The presence of a nomadic or migratory instinct hinders aggregation into permanent, large societies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Groups with long-standing hunting or pastoral habits tend to move frequently, resisting attachment to locality and thus making large, stable aggregations harder. Examples: Kookies never occupy the same place more than two or three years; Mishmees 'never name their villages'; Bachassins moved entire towns multiple times.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual capacity for cooperation (reflective intelligence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Social life presupposes intelligence that perceives benefits of cooperation and can regulate actions to effect it; lack of reflective intelligence hinders cooperation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unreflectiveness, deficient consciousness of causation, and lack of constructive imagination among the uncivilized impede effective cooperation; semi-civilized groups often show an astonishing absence of concert even in simple tasks. Example: Arab boatmen whose vocalizations do not coordinate actual pulling effort, leading to ineffective combined action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for obedience to peremptory command (authority compliance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective early cooperation often depends on obedience to strong command; this requires both emotional disposition for subordination and intellectual faith in a commander.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where cooperation initially cannot be achieved by reflective agreement, it must be enforced by peremptory command; this enforcement requires subjects' disposition to obey and an intellectual tendency to trust or believe in leaders. Thus obedience and faith in authority are evaluative criteria for the potential of political integration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credulity and religious/deified authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Credulity that leads to awe of a capable man (as possessing supernatural power) and subsequent religious control of a deified chief supports early integration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Belief in the supernatural power of chiefs and reverence for their ghosts (leading to continued obedience) can provide the social glue needed during early stages of integration. Conversely, skepticism is fatal while compulsory cooperation is necessary.
